Thinking Like an Assisted Living Manager

Should We Admit This Resident?

Screen 1 of 12
ReviewKey admission considerations
ApplyInformation to a realistic resident scenario
PracticeThinking like the manager
Goal: Move beyond “Is there a bed?” and ask whether the placement is clinically, operationally, and practically appropriate.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Welcome to Module 6, Admission and Discharge Criteria. In this lesson, we’re going to focus on one of the most important decisions an Assisted Living Manager makes: deciding whether a prospective resident is appropriate for admission. An available bed does not automatically mean an appropriate admission. As we move through this lesson, review the information that should guide the decision and then apply it to a realistic resident situation. Don’t simply look for the right answer. Think like the manager.

Before Saying “Yes”

Can we safely and appropriately meet this resident’s assessed needs?

Screen 2 of 12
1Resident Needs
→
2Resident Assessment Tool (RAT)+ current information
→
3Care Delivery CapabilityStaffing, resources, services
→
4Admission Decision
An available bed, family pressure, or hospital discharge never replaces a thoughtful admission decision.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Families sometimes need placement quickly. Hospitals may be trying to coordinate a discharge. Assisted living programs naturally want to maintain a healthy census. But those factors should not determine whether someone is appropriate for admission. First, understand the resident’s current needs. Then ask the management question: Can our program safely and appropriately meet those needs? That question should come before the move-in date, before the room assignment, and before promises are made to the family.

Critical Point

Never try to make the resident fit the available bed.

Screen 3 of 12
An Available BedDoes not automatically mean an appropriate admission.
≠
The Resident’s NeedsMust be assessed and matched to the program’s ability to provide care.
Manager mindset: Start with the resident, not the room.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

It can be tempting to begin with, “We have an opening. How can we make this work?” But the process should begin with the resident. What does this person need? What level of assistance and supervision is required? Are there medical, functional, cognitive, behavioral, or psychosocial concerns? Then look honestly at your program’s staffing, clinical support, resources, and capabilities. A thoughtful admission protects both the resident and the organization.

From the Manager’s Chair

An admission is not just a census decision.

Screen 4 of 12
Resident Safety DecisionStaffing Decision Clinical Management DecisionFamily Relations Decision Risk Management Decision
One of the best ways to prevent an inappropriate discharge later is to make a thoughtful admission decision today.
Listen & Learn
Listen to this lesson, or open Read Along below.
Read Along

Experienced managers learn that a poor admission rarely remains an admission problem. It may become a staffing problem, a medication-management problem, a family-relations problem, a resident-safety problem, or eventually, a discharge problem. One of the best ways to prevent an inappropriate discharge later is to make a thoughtful admission decision today.

Pause & Decide

Mrs. Carter needs placement tomorrow.

Screen 5 of 12

Mrs. Carter — Prospective Resident

  • Recent hospitalization
  • Three recent falls
  • Several medication changes
  • Substantial assistance with ADLs
  • Increasing nighttime confusion
“Mom has to leave the hospital tomorrow. Your facility has an opening, and we’re ready to move her in immediately.” — Mrs. Carter’s daughter
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Let’s put you in the manager’s chair. Mrs. Carter is preparing to leave the hospital. Her daughter contacts your program and tells you that her mother needs placement tomorrow. Mrs. Carter has experienced several recent falls. Her medications have changed. She now requires substantial assistance with activities of daily living, and her family reports increasing nighttime confusion. Your facility has an available room. The daughter is ready to proceed immediately. What would you do next?

Decision Feedback

Good Decision!

Screen 6 of 12
Assessment comes before admission.
We don’t have enough information to say “yes.”
✓ We have not decided that Mrs. Carter cannot be admitted.
✓ We simply need more information before making a commitment.
✓ Her daughter remains an important source of information.
✓ The next step is to understand Mrs. Carter’s current needs.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Good decision. We don’t have enough information to say yes. Notice that we haven’t decided that Mrs. Carter cannot be admitted. We simply need more information before making the commitment. Her daughter’s urgency is understandable, but urgency does not replace an appropriate admission review. Her daughter is also an important source of information. She may be able to clarify recent changes, describe how much help her mother needs, and assist us in obtaining additional information. The next step is to understand Mrs. Carter’s current needs well enough to make a responsible decision.

COMAR: From Regulation to Practice

Use the regulation to make the management decision.

Screen 7 of 12
Mrs. Carter — Regulatory Challenge

Mrs. Carter has had a recent hospitalization, three falls, medication changes, substantial ADL needs, and increasing nighttime confusion. Her daughter wants admission tomorrow.

What should guide your next decision?
Through the Surveyor’s Eyes

A surveyor reviews Mrs. Carter’s admission record six months later. What evidence would you want the record to show?

  • Current assessment information
  • Resident needs identified accurately
  • Clinical concerns addressed with the appropriate team members
  • Evidence the program could safely meet the identified needs
  • A documented rationale for the admission decision
Manager habit: Don’t memorize COMAR only for a test. Learn to use it when a real decision is in front of you.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Good managers do not treat COMAR as a separate subject that sits on a shelf. They use the regulation when decisions become difficult. In Mrs. Carter’s case, the question is not whether the family is ready or whether a bed is available. The manager needs current assessment information and must determine whether the program can safely meet her needs. Open the Regulatory Guide and notice how the preadmission and admission requirements support that decision.

Know the Whole Resident

Select the information you would want before making an admission decision.

Screen 8 of 12
Think broadly: Medical · Functional · Cognitive · Behavioral · Psychosocial · Care Delivery Capability
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Knowing that we need an assessment is one thing. Knowing what information should influence the decision is another. We need to understand Mrs. Carter as a whole person. What is her current health status? What assistance does she require throughout the day? What happens at night? What does her fall history tell us? Have there been meaningful changes in her medications or cognition? And just as importantly, can our current staffing, resources, and clinical support meet those needs? Select the information you believe should be considered.

When Distance Is a Barrier

What if the prospective resident lives out of state?

Screen 9 of 12

If a face-to-face visit is not practical before admission, consider arranging a virtual interaction with the prospective resident and family as part of the preadmission review.

During the interaction, observe:
  • General appearance and grooming
  • Alertness and engagement
  • Ability to follow one- or two-step directions
  • Ability to sit, stand, transfer, or walk, if safe
  • Communication ability
  • Calmness, irritability, anxiety, or confusion
  • Family interaction
  • Amount of assistance or cueing provided
Critical Point
Do not let distance become an excuse for making an admission decision with inadequate information.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Sometimes a prospective resident lives several states away, and a face-to-face visit simply isn’t practical. That doesn’t mean the manager should admit the resident sight unseen. Be creative. Ask the family to arrange a FaceTime, Zoom, or another video interaction. Even when the person has dementia, you may learn something useful. How is the person groomed? Do they engage with you? Can they follow a simple one- or two-step direction? If it’s safe, can they rise from a chair or take a few steps? Do they appear calm, anxious, irritable, or confused? Pay attention to how much assistance or cueing the family member provides. A virtual interaction does not replace required clinical information. It gives the manager another useful piece of the admission picture.

Regulatory Connection

Current information matters.

Screen 11 of 12
An older assessment may describe who the resident was—not who the resident is today.
Recent HospitalizationMedication ChangesFalls Functional ChangesCognitive or Behavioral Changes
Resident Assessment Tool (RAT): This tool should reflect current and reliable information to support the admission decision.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

This is where regulation and good management practice come together. Admission decisions need to be based on current information. Think again about Mrs. Carter. She has recently been hospitalized. Her medications have changed. She has fallen, and her family reports changes in cognition. An assessment that was completed much earlier may not adequately describe her now. The Resident Assessment Tool is not simply paperwork. It helps the manager and clinical team understand the resident’s current status and determine whether the program can appropriately meet those needs.

Manager Takeaway

Right Resident. Right Setting. Right Level of Care.

Screen 12 of 12
Before admission ask:
Can we safely, consistently, and appropriately meet this resident’s needs?
You are ready to complete this lesson when you can:
  • Explain why thoughtful admission decisions protect the resident, family, staff, and organization.
  • Identify the key information needed before making an admission decision.
Listen & Learn
Read Along

Let’s finish with one principle. Good admissions don’t happen simply because everything looks acceptable on paper. They happen because someone asked the right questions, obtained current information, collaborated with the appropriate people, and honestly evaluated the program’s ability to provide care. Remember: Right resident. Right setting. Right level of care. When those three align, we’ve created the foundation for a safer placement, a better resident experience, and a stronger assisted living program.

Module 6 Regulatory Guide — Admission Decision

Preadmission — What should you establish before saying “yes”?

  • Obtain and review the required medical and functional assessment information.
  • Evaluate medical, functional, cognitive, behavioral, psychosocial, and nutritional status.
  • Determine whether the resident’s needs can be safely met within the facility’s licensed level of care.
  • Assess whether awake overnight staff are needed and document that determination when indicated.
  • Use current health information; the Resident Assessment Tool should be completed within the applicable regulatory timeframe.
Manager test: What do I still need to know about Mrs. Carter before I can responsibly commit to admission?

Admission — What makes the decision appropriate?

  • The resident’s assessed needs must be safely met within the program’s licensed level of care.
  • Admission decisions should be based on objective assessment findings and the program’s demonstrated ability to provide safe, appropriate care.
  • Clinical and behavioral needs that cannot be safely managed should not be accepted simply because a room is available.
  • The manager should explain honestly what the program can and cannot provide.
  • Document the rationale supporting the admission decision.
Manager test: If I had to explain this admission to a surveyor six months from now, could I show why it was reasonable?

Through the Surveyor’s Eyes

Survey review commonly focuses on whether required assessments were completed, resident needs were identified accurately, and the program admitted only residents whose needs could be safely met.

Think like the surveyor: What in the record proves that the decision was based on current resident needs rather than census pressure, family urgency, or convenience?

Resident Assessment Tool (RAT) — Virtual Notebook Preview

As you preview the RAT, notice:

Admission decisions rely on much more than a diagnosis. The tool brings together medical, functional, cognitive, behavioral, psychosocial, medication, and safety information.

Pages 3–4:
Look for mobility, ADLs, fall risk, psychosocial needs, and overnight supervision. How could these findings influence an admission decision?
